title: Minimax Value of Waiting for Rare Subgroup Counts before Allocating Assay Budgets
banked_reason: Sound proposal after typed-strategy repair, but D-0.5 assessed letter-tier finite-game benchmark below the required field novelty floor; no in-scope field frontier survived independent consultation.
gap_reasons: tier=letter below novelty_target=field: the strongest result is an exact finite-game benchmark and separation from proposal-defined heuristics, not a matched rate, sharper named published bound, first bound for a named method/estimand, efficiency result with attaining estimator, or coverage result.

The stated finite-class minimax equality, attainment, and least-favorable-prior structure are standard finite statistical-game results already covered by Berger1985; retain them as cited infrastructure rather than a novelty-bearing theorem.
proof_attempt_summary: Discovery tested an exact finite-cohort and marked-Poisson post-count assay allocation benchmark, then pivoted to a finite-game strict-adaptation criterion. A deterministic repair defined randomized strategies and induced risks; the next D-0.5 review found no soundness flag but assessed only letter-tier novelty, below the required field floor. No Stage 0 derivation or Lean proof was attempted; a field-level rate or common-model published-method comparison would require a new research architecture.
tldr: The proposal characterizes strict minimax value of waiting for rare subgroup counts before allocating a fixed additional noncase-assay budget. Its conflict modulus ranges over the complete fixed-design least-favorable set and tests whether a single precommitment, capped by eligibility in each count state, is conditionally Bayes optimal. A two-state certificate gives checkable sufficient conditions. A nondegenerate neighborhood of exact eight-law, three-stratum experiments targets positive finite-risk enclosures for post-count improvement and for separation from proposal-defined Hamilton case-balance and Wright-inspired allocations, with every risk evaluated on the same eight laws. These rules are informed by Tao--Zeng--Lin and Yang et al.; their published optimality claims remain tied to their own efficiency criteria. The open question concerns exposure-mark feedback and canonical minimax geometry.
gap: Regular two-phase design theorems optimize semiparametric variance or information criteria, while a favorable Bayes gap for one prior does not establish strict minimax value of count timing.
fill: An attained finite minimax dual yields the capped-precommitment strictness criterion, a two-state conflict certificate, and an invariant support face. An asymmetric finite-law neighborhood supplies matched-risk comparison targets for two completely specified allocation rules.
